posts.content_md: > **Hans:** JohnFP wrote:The slit allows good parallax in the horizontal direction but restricts the smear in the vertical direction, just like a rainbow hologram. Having the tube oriented in the vertical direction (with respect to a horizontal slit..This makes an interesting scenario. Suppose you would make a H2 through a horizontal AND a vertical slit. You would have full parallax in both directions. But would you still have no distortion when you view it diagonally? If not, it would seem that all the other information from a full H2 copy would be superfluous. So, in that case, would it not be possible to make a reflection H2 much brighter by using only a horizontal and vertical slit (cross slit) in front of the H2? There would be much less information to store in the holographic plate. Has anyone ever tried this?

posts.content_md: > **JohnFP:** Wow Hans, I like it!!!Well, I have some thoughts and could not explain the properly so I decided an illustration may help.This is very interesting to think about. So in the full double slit as you move left to right at cent of hologram you get horizontal parallax until one eye is alligned with the veritcal slit. I would then imaging you would see the blur as in a full master hologram. And as you move up and down with eyes close to center I would imaging a 2D image. But if you moved up or down at the extreem left or right you may not see anything until one eye can see through the verical slit and then again only a 2D image would be seen. BUT...How about the last drawing? Would not both eyes see a differnt slit perspective and preserve the vertical paralax?Hans this is totally cool and exciting. It just so happens I made a couple of 8x10 master that I want to copy and I may have to give this a try. If you or anyone else tries it, please post your findings here, or better yet, start a new thread.

posts.post_subject: Crisper, Deeper H2 Reflections using a slit.
posts.content_md:
You can mock up the effect on parallax without shooting a hologram by cutting out masks and putting them on top of a H1 and viewing the virtual image.

Guys like Randy Jame and Lon Moore got brighter and sharper H2's by illuminating only the central part of their masters. Of course, there wasn't too much in the way of parallax.

posts.post_subject: Crisper, Deeper H2 Reflections using a slit.
posts.content_md:
> **Ed Wesly:** Of course, there wasn't too much in the way of parallax.

There wasn't too much in the way of **vertical** parallax. This wasn't often missed in those cases as most were intended to be hung on a wall and people tend not to jump up and down when looking at something hanging in front of them.
